Author: @GENSHIN11
Content:
Black Hole (BH) 🕳️

    Boundary: Defined by the Event Horizon, a one-way surface beyond which escape is impossible.

    Core: Contains a Singularity, a point of infinite density where all mass is crushed and the laws of physics break down.

    Interior State: Gravitational pull is relentlessly inward, resulting in complete collapse of matter.

    Observability: Confirmed objects supported by strong observational evidence (gravitational waves, accretion disk X-rays, shadow imaging).

    Paradoxes: Associated with theoretical problems like the Information Paradox (information is seemingly lost) and the existence of a singularity.

Gravastar (Hypothetical) ✨

    Boundary: Features a Thin Shell of exotic matter or ultra-relativistic fluid, lying just where the event horizon would be. There is no true event horizon.

    Core: Consists of a Dark Energy Core (a false vacuum) that generates a powerful negative pressure.

    Interior State: The core's negative pressure perfectly balances the inward force of gravity, preventing complete collapse.

    Observability: Remains purely hypothetical; proposed as a theoretical alternative, but current gravitational wave data aligns better with the black hole model.

    Paradoxes: Proposed specifically to resolve the singularity problem and the information paradox by offering a stable, non-singular endpoint for stellar collapse.

Content: I think gravastar is an interesting speculative alternative to black holes, but current physics suggests it's not a stable long-term solution for objects with extreme mass. Author: @mutaharjamallaskar5006
Content:
🔥 Intro: Black Hole se bhi zyada dangerous?

Video ke start mein kaha gaya ki ho sakta hai ek aisi cheez ho jo black hole ko bhi destroy kar sakti ho — aur uska naam hai Gravastar.

Yeh ek aisa object hai jo pure energy se bhara hota hai, aur iska outer shell ek bahut hi strange aur extreme matter se bana hota hai.


---

💥 Massive Star ki Death aur Gravastar ka Janm:

Jab koi bahut bada star mar jaata hai, to wo supernova me explode karta hai. Uske baad do possibilities hoti hain:

1. Neutron Star banta hai (agar mass kam ho).


2. Black Hole banta hai (agar mass zyada ho).



Lekin Gravastar ek third aur aur bhi zyada weird option hai.

Black hole jahan singularity (infinite density) mein collapse karta hai, Gravastar mein matter itna compress hota hai ki wo energy mein badal jaata hai. Jaise ek mini-universe create ho raha ho jo phir expand karne lagta hai.

Iss expanding energy bubble aur collapsing star ke shell ke beech ek extreme fight hoti hai — ek taraf unstoppable expansion, aur doosri taraf collapsing gravity. Is intense battle ke baad ek new type ka material banta hai jo Gravastar ka shell banata hai.


---

🌌 Gravastar kaisa dikhta hai?

Size: London jitna area le sakta hai.

Mass: 10 Suns ke barabar.

Shell:

Bahut cold — sirf ek billionth degree above absolute zero.

Itna tight ki 1 meter stretch karne ke liye poori ek supernova ki energy chahiye.

Banaya gaya hai ek unknown exotic material se.




---

🌀 Andar kya hai?

Gravastar ka interior completely empty hai. Koi particle, atom ya light nahi — ek perfect vacuum.

Lekin yeh khaali jagah bhi bohot powerful hai, kyunki yeh vacuum energy se bhara hua hai — ek compressed version of the fundamental vacuum fluid jisme se saari particles aati hain.

Yeh compressed vacuum billion trillion trillion trillion times zyada energetic hota hai normal vacuum se.


---

🧠 Vacuum kya hota hai? (Easy example se):

Particles (jaise quarks, photons) asal mein waves hote hain ek invisible ocean mein — is ocean ko hi vacuum kehte hain.

Yeh vacuum hamesha hota hai, chaahe usmein particles ho ya na ho.

Gravastar ke andar yeh ocean itna zyada compress hota hai ki usmein aur compression possible nahi hota.


Shell is vacuum ko bahar nikalne nahi deta. Dono extreme forces — shell aur energy — ek dusre ko balance karte hain, isliye Gravastar stable rehta hai.


---

👀 Gravastar vs Black Hole (Outside se dono same lagte hain):

Dono light trap karte hain.

Dono ke paas huge mass hota hai.

Dono time ko slow karte hain.

Lekin Gravastar ke paas ek physical shell hoti hai, jabki black hole ke paas sirf ek event horizon.


Agar koi Gravastar ke andar girega:

Pehle hi gravity ke pressure se mar jaayega.

Uske baad atoms shell ko touch karke dissolve ho jaayenge.

Wo energy mein convert hoke Gravastar ko thoda aur bada aur heavy bana denge.



---

❓ Phir point kya hai?

Kya yeh sirf ek imaginary idea hai?

> Bilkul nahi — Black holes bhi ek time pe sirf theory the. Scientists ne unhe papers aur equations mein suggest kiya tha, aur dheere-dheere proof milte gaye.



Same way, Gravastar bhi ek valid theory hai, jiska proof shayad future mein mile.


---

🔍 Gravastar aur Black Hole ko kaise alag pehchanein?

Jab do black holes collide karte hain to ek bass drum jaise deep sound create hota hai.

Lekin do Gravastars milte hain to ek gong jaise echo hoti hai (jo thodi der tak rehti hai).

Scientists gravitational wave detectors ka use karke in echoes ko sunne ki koshish kar rahe hain, lekin abhi technology utni sensitive nahi hai.


---

🧪 Conclusion:

Gravastars:

Black holes ke problems (jaise singularities, information loss) ko solve karte hain.

But unke khud ke bhi naye problems hain (jaise exotic matter ki zarurat).

Wo reality ho bhi sakte hain, ya sirf ek theory bhi ho sakti hai.


Lekin science ka maqsad hi hai naye ideas explore karna — aur Gravastar ek aisa idea hai jo hume universe ke asli nature tak le jaa sakta hai.

Author: @achimgebhardt5982
Content: The idea of the singularity and the infinite density in the core of a black hole comes from the general theory of relativity and the fact that mathematical infinities are encountered. However, it is unlikely that this represents reality, because we have no means of describing the state at the center of a black hole. The general theory of relativity loses its validity in black holes, so mathematical results from it are also invalid. It is still one of the unsolved mysteries of physics, but only a theory of quantum gravity could allow valid assumptions about the interior of black holes. It is very likely that the singularity and many other phenomena that are popularly attributed to the interior of black holes are pure fantasies and that we are rather talking about an unknown form of matter with finite density that can possibly only exist in an extraordinarily deformed space-time. But - as I said - everything that is said today about the interior of black holes is pure speculation and very probably far away from reality.

Author: @DavidConnerCodeaholic
Content:
I’m skeptical. If “E=mcc”, then how does the vacuum energy retain equilibrium with the energy of the collapsing mass? It’s all basically just energy at that point. That’s not to say that it’s impossible for the two forces to maintain equilibrium after it’s established, particularly without needing to worry about the tiniest impact or imperfections “popping the bubble.” After formation, it’s more about the relative magnitudes of forces.

To answer the above, the concentration of mass pushing into the center during collapse would need a counteracting vacuum energy that doesn’t change even though the relative density of matter (globally) does change. The mechanisms by which vacuum energy is “concentrated” are unclear to me.

A well known ideal case for gravitational energy in physics is that inside a sphere of uniformly & continuously distributed mass, the gravitational potential is zero.

Author: @Geeknificent
Content:
Please do not perpetuate fallacies about black holes having qualities that are "infinite"

The first major fallacy of a black hole is the name itself. Black holes are not actually holes, but instead, like neutron stars, are a stellar body that breaks down mass to a subatomic level, just to a more extreme degree than neutron stars do. 

Both can have accretion disks, jet cones, both have an axis, and even a spin. 

Use of Infinity in describing a black is one of the second major fallacies that creates a poor understanding of what a black hole is as no qualities about a black hole is infinite. They have measurable mass and therfore volume and density is also finite. This also means their gravity is finite too otherwise if they had infinite gravity it would cause the universe to collapse.

Absolutely no qualities about a black hole can be reasonably described as infinite without the math resulting in the universe being consumed by a stellar body that isn't actually a hole to begin with.

Also just because blackheads bend or distort time and space around them does not mean they break physics.

The law of zero point energy exists everywhere in the universe and black holes are subject to this as well. The universe maintains an equilibrium in all things, so eventually when a black hole evaporates in billions of years the physics in that area would return to normal as the universe is essentially elastic when it comes to physics, it can bend but not break.

If black holes ever broke physics that returns to another scenario where the universe collapses/disintegrates/permanently stops working.

Similarly, with the gravistar, what you are describing is a theoretical maximal point energy scenario. Where space has become so inflated that the interior of the gravity is empty and nothing but space. While in theory this is possible, it would have to be met with a zero point energy as well in this scenario. Meaning the surface of it would essentially be a black hole in order to keep it stable, otherwise the force of the expanded space inside the gravity just blows it apart entirely.

That would mean all "black holes" in the universe are either, super dense stellar bodies that suck in light, or gravistars, that would also suck in light. As such in both scenarios there would be no way to distinguish between the two simply from observing the exterior. 

The elasticity of space would demand that a maximal energy point be met with azero energy point to remain coherent.

But there's a major flaw in this scenario where a maximal energy point is contained by a zero energy point. They would cancel each other out and cause matter to scatter and dissipate since you have a zero value and a max value next to each other, they would essentially summarize and force localized space into equilibrium sending matter everywhere, probably turning the star into a nebula again as matter is shredded.

Dark energy is just a subtle wind of garlic-scented quantum broth, gently pushing the bowls apart, causing the universe to expand. Now, you might be wondering: where does supersymmetry fit into this? Cosmology? It's the recipe book of the universe. Black holes become potholes in the cosmic pasta sheet. Wormholes? Author: @chrisjager5370
Content:
As I understand it, we can't ever see anything fall across the event horizon of a black hole, from outside we'd see its rate of change go to zero and any light it gives redshifted to zero energy. There'd be a shell just outside the event horizon of the black hole were we lost track of the particle falling in. If anything, what we'd see is the event horizon expanding past the particle, or at least the Schwarzschild radius of black hole plus particle becomes large enough to encompass the particle. From the perspective of the particle, it would fall straight through the event horizon without noticing it was there. Both are the same thing described from a different perspective.

Anyhow, it's nice to see there's a structure very similar to black holes, without a lot of their weirdness, with a whole lot of new and different weirdness instead.

Author: @KyleDentonOfficial
Content:
I'm not a physicist by any means, but I have some concerns. I absolutely adore alternate theories, like Gravastars, and I think this video is extremely valid especially considering the modern black hole theory has its massive flaw (the singularity). However, I think there are some points that this video should have mentioned that are very important! Gravastars can’t spin.

Which is critical for the whole concept. Maintaining the balance between the inner vacuum and the outer shell looks like it's a big issue. The thin shell of a gravastar needs to perfectly counteract the vacuum energy inside, and it could become unstable over time. Currently, because of centripetal force, if the gravastar spun it would tear itself apart. The theory needs more work, and I believe that should have been a larger point in the video.

Besides that, I really liked this video and would love to see more about gravastars. You could ask similar questions to those in your previous black hole videos, like what might happen if gravastars collide using the current math, or whether quasi-stars work with the gravastar theory. Also, other alternate black hole theories or alternate science in general, like dark-energy stars, which get a little abstract.

Author: @x_MoonlitShade
Content:
Gravastars are a dope concept but I feel like there’s a couple of things Kurtzesagt left out. For one, he mentions how they are so similar to black holes that they’re basically indistinguishable, and talks about them as if they’d exist alongside black holes, but fails to mention that the theory of them was actually proposed as an alternative to black holes. It’s likely all black holes are regular black holes with an event horizon, or gravastars, but both existing is probably less likely. That’s not to say that one’s existence excludes the other, though. 

Also there’s the concept of Nestars, or nested gravastars, which are gravastars with another gravastar inside of them like a matryoshka doll. 

Also the inside of a gravastar is a false vacuum. You’ve done a video on false vacuum decay before but, yeah, wouldn’t want to pop one of these “soap bubbles.”

Content: if I understood the concept correctly, it is meant to give a singularity-free explanation for all the observable phenomena which are usually associated with black holes, i.e. it is an alternative theory for black holes. but I have never understood the issue with black holes. the singularities are not problematic at all, except for Kerr's metric, but that's for unreal black holes with zero angular momentum. real black holes have non-zero angular momentum and thus their singularities are not point-like objects with zero dimensional mass distribution, but line-like (ring-like) objects with one dimensional mass distribution. I just don't see any reason to replace our concept of black holes with this new concept which doesn't actually explain anything but brings and raises further questions.

Author: @DrewishAF
Content:
One thing that irritates me about these wild cosmological obects is the terminology we use to attempt to describe them. For example: "information" being "destroyed" by "black holes." Those words have very specific meanings outside the context of cosmology/theoretical physics, but suddenly gain slightly different meanings once used in this context. 

Of course, I understand that certain words were chosen as they are the most similar to the actual definition and can give some notion of the concept to people outside the field. But it does create a lot of confusion, misunderstanding, and can serve as the basis for flawed/inaccurate arguments. 

Think about it, how are you supposed to accurately convey the concept of "vacuum energy" and it's density to the layperson who only hears the logical oxymoron of "energy in nothingness." Hell, I understand more of this than the average person (yet far less than those who've dedicated their lives to this area of study, of course) and even I have difficulty actually explaining certain concepts because my own everyday usage of certain terms bogs me down. I just think we might be better served by trying to utilize new terms without so much baggage (which is, itself, an idiom) rather than recycling pre-existing terms for the sake of brevity/ease.

Content:
Technically there are 4 outcomes 1. Planetary nebula: smaller then 7 solar masses. This nebula creates the materials everything is made of and often creates planets in the explosion aftermath. 2. Neutron star: neutron stars are created at 7-25 solar masses. This number is on the border between a neutron star and a white dwarf but depending on factors like the stars core mass, it could become a neutron star at 7 solar masses but it is unlikely. Stars at 8 solar masses are almost always bound to become neutron stars. Neutron stars are extremely dense and could have strange matter in there core. The strongest material in the universe is the crust of a neutron star. Neutron stars are created in supernovas. 
3. Black holes. Black holes are created when a star 10-30 solar masses. This depends on the core mass of the star as do black holes but this is traditionally the total mass of the star.
4. Proposed gravastars. Highly theoretical. But still definitely possible.
Bonus: in planetary nebula explosions the star could turn into a white dwarf if large enough.
White dwarfs live significantly longer than other stars and also spin very fast like neutron stars.

Author: @isatousarr7044
Content:
In the intriguing realm of cosmic physics, black holes have long been seen as the ultimate enigmas of the universe. With their immense gravitational pull and event horizons from which nothing, not even light, can escape, black holes are the dark beacons of deep space. However, an equally fascinating concept known as gravastars has emerged as a theoretical counterpart, or "evil twin," to black holes, challenging the conventional understanding of these cosmic giants.

Gravastars, short for gravitational vacuum stars, propose an alternative structure to that of black holes. Instead of an event horizon and an infinitely dense singularity at their core, gravastars are theorized to have an exotic state of matter or energy that prevents the formation of a singularity. This boundary, often described as a thin shell of exotic matter, is supported by the intense pressure generated from the vacuum energy inside. Such a structure would result in a compact object with a dense core and an outer shell that could reflect or bend light, making them theoretically distinguishable from black holes.

The concept of gravastars arises from solutions to Einstein's equations in general relativity that don't necessarily require a singularity to explain the extreme gravitational fields we observe. Instead of collapsing into an infinite density point, the matter inside a gravastar remains in a stable state, and the object maintains its physical integrity, avoiding the gravitational singularity associated with black holes. This suggests that the inner workings of the object might allow for a different kind of gravitational behavior and potentially avoid some of the paradoxes that black holes present, such as the information paradox.

The study of gravastars not only expands our understanding of how massive objects can form and evolve but also raises questions about the nature of dark energy and the role of exotic matter in the cosmos. If gravastars exist, they could provide an alternative explanation for some phenomena typically attributed to black holes, like the behavior of gamma-ray bursts or gravitational wave sources. 


Observationally, gravastars would be difficult to distinguish from black holes due to their similar effects on surrounding matter and space. However, as our technology advances and we develop more sophisticated methods for observing gravitational waves and light emissions from near these objects, we may gain insight into whether gravastars exist as a legitimate cosmic structure or remain a fascinating theoretical idea.

In essence, gravastars represent a new frontier in cosmic physics, a realm where the known boundaries of matter, gravity, and the fabric of spacetime are pushed to their limits. If these objects exist, they could reshape our understanding of gravity, black holes, and the nature of the universe itself.

Author: @TheAruruu
Content:
Ok, I can wrap my head around the concept of vacuum fluid, and the concept of pressurizing to create a vacuum that has unbelievable energy (and therefore mass), and I can even accept that the shell would be almost incalculably thin and durable. What I don't understand is what keeps them stable. For a star, it's a simple battle between gravity pressing in and pressure pushing out. For a black hole, the singularity is basically a hole that is punched into the fabric of reality that only barely exists in the first place, where gravity has completely won, making it a self-sustaining object (for the most part, it still needs to eat to maintain itself, but black hole evaporation is fairly well understood). 

What I'm missing from the gravastar puzzle is the thing that sustains the shell. Is it just an intrinsic property of that as-of-yet-unnamed substance that makes up the shell?
I've also got a few questions about the shell. If 2 gravastars can collide and apparently merge, then the shell substance can move and deform. Assuming that this shell does not require the pressure of the interior to exist, that should mean it can be separated from the gravastar in theory (gravity would obviously make doing this nearly impossible). If it can be separated, would it still have the matter destroying/converting properties that the shell around a gravastar has? If the shell is so thin that it makes atoms look gigantic, and the shell converts mass directly into energy to be pumped into the interior, would a gravastar that consumes a lot of matter without interacting with another gravastar have a thinner shell than a gravastar that just merged with another gravastar? Can the shell get thin enough to fail? Is the shell thickness at the planck scale, or is it larger than that?

Also, what happens when a black hole and a gravastar encounter each other? Would the singularity be consumed by the shell, converting its entire mass instantaneously into energy since a singularity has a dimension of zero, and the shell is thinner than atoms, the time it would take for the singularity to pass through the shell... well, what ever counts as time at these insane gravitational levels anyway... would be effectively zero? If the black hole 'wins', would the shell break, dumping that energy and 'vacuum fluid' into the black hole, or would it bleed off into the space around the black hole?

Author: @gregorywalpole8442
Content:
Basically, your math teacher lied to you. The universe is *not* math, nor does it run on math. Math is a system of logic humans created to simulate the universe, and while it's very accurate and generally good enough for most things we need it for, it is not *perfect*. Math allows things the universe seemingly does not, such as perfect circles, infinite division, negative numbers, and things like graphed singularities and vertical asymptotes being used to describe anything physical. 

Black holes work as a mathematic concept, but do things we're pretty sure the universe doesn't actually allow due to being a singularity. Gravastars are an attempt at a different model that should fit the same requirements and show similar external behavior but eliminate that pesky singularity in favor of the universe hitting a certain limit and saying "knock it off; you can't take this any farther".

This video is severely misrepresenting quantum physics; and for no better reason than they don't want to explain quantum physics all over again.
The double slit experiment showed that photons exist as both particles and waves, and later experiments showed that this is actually true of everything on a small scale. So a space where there are only waves and no particles is not a vacuum or void or empty at all, it is just a space where the stuff never has to behave like a particle.
No modern physicist describes vacuum as the medium for these waves, rather they say that the waves don't need a medium. So it is not vacuum inside the Gravastar.

Content: Wiki: A gravastar is an object hypothesized in astrophysics by Pawel O. Mazur and Emil Mottola as an alternative to the black hole theory. It has usual black hole metric outside of the horizon, but de Sitter metric inside. On the horizon there is a thin shell of matter. The term "gravastar" is a portmanteau of the words "gravitational vacuum star". This solution of Einstein equations is stable and has no singularities.[1] Further theoretical considerations of gravastars include the notion of a nestar (a second gravastar nested within the first one).

Content: How would matter smashing into the shell add to its internal volume? Is the suggestion that the space between the bits of matter gets absorbed through the shell for some reason? Then, over time, the shell would get thicker and denser and it'd extert more & more pressure on the nothing inside it (along with itself) until it would overwhelm it, collapse, & turn into a singularity anyway. Or.. it'd crack before that and the vacuum rushing out would carry the stuff in the broken shell with it, creating essentially a new big bang. The shell stuff would be stretched out by the expanding vacuum carrying it off & turn back into normal matter as it rapidly absorbs heat & expands from moving so fast. All heat within reach of the explosion would be absorbed by the shell fragments, wiping out anything already there. It'd basically be a big reset switch much like everything being sucked into a singularity, except more horrifying because you'd be aware of it happening..

Since this happens at the limit of what considered outside the horizon, we should see in some way the resulting flash it would cause. But we observed matter falling into black holes (e.g. GRS 1915+105) and we only observed a deeming in light when it fell on the dark object, which can only be explained if it is "substracted" by a black hole horizon. This doesn't rule out gravastars as both objects may exist, but I think it's not quite in favor of their existence. Same goes for fuzzballs.

Author: @JanasV
Content:
Kurzg, as much as I love your videos, this one just contradicts itself over and over again. Let's go in order:

Statements:
  1 - How a gravastar is born:
    1.1 (pure energy bubble) - The core of it is made up of atoms and particles that are crushed up so violently that they "become" pure energy, that wants to expand.
    1.2 (the shell) - The opposing forces of the "pure energy bubble" (which is expanding) and the collapsing star (which is pulling itself to the center under its own gravity) create a shell out of a new kind of material that "we don't know what it is, but we know it is possible".
  2 - Composition and technical specifications of a gravastar
    2.1 (temperature) - a *billionth* of a degree above absolute zero (about -459.67°F or 0°K)
    2.2 (the shell) - Is made out of an entirely new kind of matter, that doesn't consist of atoms, doesn't have a name yet, and its thickness is less than that of a single atom. Which is supposedly the reason why it is so cold. The shell is seemingly unbreakable, unmovable, can't be deformed or stretched in any way, unless acted upon by a force comparable to a supernova.
    2.3 (the interior/core) - Is made up of "super condensed nothingness" or vacuum.
    2.4 (self behavior) - The interior or core wants to stretch outwards (or grow in volume), but the limiting factor is the shell, which itself is at the physical limits of what's possible.
    2.5 (perception) - To our perception, gravastars are perfectly black, eternal objects with insane amounts of mass, that are cold to the literal limit, therefore they look and behave exactly like black holes.
    2.6 (mass) - Any additional mass that comes close enough to a gravastar, will be ripped apart and ground down by the gravitational forces. Once those remains touch the shell, the atoms will "probably dissolve completely" to be converted into the vacuum energy of the interior, making the gravastar slightly bigger and massive.

The problem (statements contradict previous statements):
  1.1, 1.2, 2.3, 2.4 and 2.6 contradict each other; by your statements, the interior is trying to *grow in volume or expand*, but you called the interior "super condensed nothingness" and a vacuum, and said that the inside of the gravastar has incredibly stronger vacuum than the surrounding space (which basically means that the pressure on the inside is a lot lower than on the outside), and as we all know, in that case the higher pressure of the outside acts in a way that the object should want to *shrink or decrease in volume* to even out the pressures inside and outside the object as much as possible. Also, now that we established that lower pressure (inside the shell) wants to shrink the shell around it, and not expand it, statement 2.6 makes no sense, as the "dissolved" matter from the outside "would add to the vacuum energy inside" which means it would lower the pressure even further, which would decrease the size and volume of the gravastar, but you stated that the pressure is at its lowest possible limit and that the gravastar would grow in size and mass, and if it would grow in size, that would mean that the shell's area would need to increase and the interior's volume would need to increase, too, and then there's statement 2.2 which says that in order for the shell to deform or stretch in any way, it would take the force of at least a supernova to do that.


I'm not saying you're the one who's misinforming people, it may be the source. Either way I hope I'm wrong and that you can correct me and explain where I'm wrong.
Best wishes.

Author: @Dolkarr
Content:
Not sure if I'm not understanding something or if there is a small mistake at 6:56 - "If you fell onto a gravastar, you would be extremely dead before you even hit the surface"
The source document elaborates with "From the outside, a gravastar behaves basically like a black hole until the point you have already almost hit the surface."
But we can reach the event horizon of supermassive black holes without any spaghettification. Gravastars don't have an event horizon, so their surface must lie beyond where a black hole's event horizon would be. This should mean either that we can also reach the surface of a supermassive gravastar, or that such gravastars don't exist and any black supermassive objects are still black holes. The latter would make them kind of disappointing as an idea to replace the problems that black holes have.

Author: @floridamangaming2453
Content:
Ok, so what if, and hear me out... "vacuum" is actually dark matter/energy?

We already know space is constantly creating pairs of matter and antimatter that instantly annihilate (we've  even created them in a lab), releasing energy. So what if this sea of nothing is actually a sea of particles that exist for fractions of milliseconds, and carries normal matter with it as it expands and shrinks, and could be what gravitational waves travel through?

My hypothesis is that the energy produced by annihilation is greater than the gravity between the pairs *(universe expanding, and gravity being a weak force in general)*, so they push each other away. But, if there's a large collection of normal matter, like a star or galaxy/supermassive black hole, its gravity can add to the gravity of these temporary particle pairs to the point where the gravity between them overcomes the energy from annihilation, pulling more of them in, drawing other objects made of normal matter with them.

Perhaps a gravastar is where the density of these pairs is so great, the energy of annihilation simply creates more pairs which also annihilate, creating more pairs in a repeating cycle until the end of time. At densities this extreme, the gravity of the pairs would equal the energy if annihilation, so instead of an unstoppable force fighting an immovable object, it's two unstoppable forces fighting, creating an immovable object between them (the shell) (no idea how black holes factor in. Maybe when big stars die, they always create a gravastar, and black holes are the result of gravity winning, and supernovas are the result of the energy winning, but I don't think this is the case)

I could be wrong about all of this, as this isn't the most researched thing (it is just a hypothesis after all). It's just something I've cobbled together from various documentaries and youtube videos, so feedback is appreciated, and if I'm completely wrong, feel free to let me know

Author: @ArchTeryx00
Content:
One of the most interesting cosmology lessons Kurzgesagt ever made. There are a couple of thoughts that come to mind, one real, one fictional:

A huge plot point in David Brin's "Earth," is that humanity figured out a way to create tiny black holes from vacuum energy - enormous quantities of matter from nothing. Unlimited cheap energy! We've created miniature gravistars! Until we accidentally let one go into the mantle of the planet.

That turns out to not be such a big deal because it's too small to be self-sustaining. It dissipates back to vacuum energy. But it reveals a *much larger* black hole inside the Earth's core, put there by alien forces, that's meant as a doomsday machine. That second black hole, named "Beta," *also* acts like a gravistar. After a frantic bit of research, we figure out how to use gravity lasers - focused gravity waves - to push Beta into thinner matter, so it loses and gains mass at the same rate. Earth is saved! But then things get truly, truly weird. Suddenly everyone has weapons more powerful than nuclear bombs, and what exactly *is* Beta doing inside the Earth's crust? It isn't eating the planet, but it's changing its matter the way a gravistar would - with entirely unexpected results. It turns out, the origin of Beta and its intended effects on our planet are far weirder than we ever imagined...

It's a very interesting read in the context of this video!

The other is that you know what else was created out of vacuum energy? The Big Bang! If we ever are to actually discover gravistars and analyze the nature of their matter - *quark* matter - we might help answer the questions of dark energy, dark matter, and the Big Bang itself.

Finally, fantastic job explaining things that pretty much can only be explained with complex calculus. If your universe is only mathematic models, things can truly get weird. But sometimes... weird also happens to be true.

Author: @katherinek6166
Content: The big problem the gravastars *might* address is the final parsec problem. Unlike other problems with black holes which might just come down to, "They're just weird," the final parsec is well within the realms of classical physics. It's the problem of two black holes orbiting each other merging. Two regular stars orbiting each other generate a lot of drag that causes them to approach. Black holes, being point objects, don't. The pair orbiting each other will only lose energy to gravity, and that takes a very long time. Too long for supermassive black holes to have formed in our universe. Gravastars could have tidal interactions that speed this up dramatically.

Author: @Tricosis.
Content: Worth noting that gravastars and black holes are the same thing. People typically envision the singularity model when describing  a black hole, in which past the event horizon, space and time is bent to potentially infinite proportions. But anything past the event horizon is entirely theoretical. Gravastars would also produce an event horizon. Both models would look and function like black holes, but past the event horizon may lie a gravastar instead of a singularity. It's a little hard to verify which model is correct, since we can't retrieve any information that are locked behind the event horizon.

Author: @Electru522
Content:
I've studied astronomy all my life, and this is complete news to me. But it's also an answer to something I've been struggling to comprehend for awhile now....that being the singularity itself.

Simply put, the universe does not deal in infinites. The definition of infinity is something without an ending point, and no matter where we look, no matter what experiments we conduct, no matter what simulations we run, over and over again, EVERYTHING has some kind of limit. Whether that be a breaking point, or a point where it is simply impossible to add any more energy to the system. And yet, singularities are stated to have infinite density, infinite temperature, and be infinitely small. No wonder they break all our laws of physics, because we are trying to impose a divide-by-zero scenario, a mathematical question mark onto reality. 

But this fixes ALL of that. Compressed vacuum energy encased in a subatomic thick shell of crystalized pure energy. You can have the same kind of insane mass and gravity that black holes have, still apply all the whacky light bending nonsense that black holes are known for, and even solve the information paradox along the way (of which the answer for the information paradox is oddly similar to this!)

But I do see 2 potential problems, though, with the first being Hawking Radiation. Hawking's discovery essentially requires the use of an event horizon, so if you have a shell of crystalized pure energy, how does it shrink to transfer energy to the one escaping binary particle? And if said shell is effectively indestructible, then the roundabout answer for Hawking Radiation of the vacuum energy leaking out of the shell doesn't make sense either. So, if gravastars are the answer to the singularity....we're essentially led back to the eternal black hole problem that Hawking Radiation solved.

The second problem is them colliding. What happens if one them cracks open? Can they even be cracked open with the energy of a collision? If not, do they just.....smush together like soap bubbles do? Thankfully, this is something that could hopefully be answered by just a bit more research into the subject, and I imagine that these collisions could provide an answer for Gamma Ray Bursts, if I'm to guess!

Content:
I have a problem with the existence of neutron stars being measurable, and then leaping from the perfectly measurable gravity of a neutron star to the so-called infinite gravity of a black hole when it only takes a few times more than mass and gravity of a neutron star to make a black hole. 

The smallest known black hole has about 3.8 times the mass of our Sun. Yet people will describe its gravity as being infinite just because light can't escape from it and nothing you know could escape from it. The inability of light to escape is not a suitable test for infinite power. Light is way faster than us, but it's not light can be absorbed and bent in many ways. Just because a black hole off resident environment for spiraling orbit, it doesn't suggest infinity at play. 

I know I'm going to get jumped on, but it seems that there's a lot of official hyperbolic lore associated with black holes and supernovae. We are only just breaking away from the notion that it takes a supernova to make a black hole. We're only starting to become comfortable with the notion of primordial black holes, which formfrom the sheer weight of mass, and not a supernova. 

I'm saying that there's a difference between extreme and infinite. Just because our math breaks, it doesn't mean that reality or space and time have to also break.

Here is a simple test. You have two incredibly large black holes orbiting each other. They eventually merge and become one larger black hole. At any point of this union, did either black hole break apart? Can the holy black hole bifurcate as they join together? Can their shape change at all?

Is it possible to break apart a black hole? If not, then how can two become one? How can Sagittarius A exist without gobbling up other black holes en masse? 

When you ask a modern scientist this question, a paradox ensues because black holes supposedly have size, but they're also considered to be mere points. The earth would be the size of a plum as a black hole, but for some arguments some would also say that it's a point, with no size.

For me, the answer is simple. The black hole must bifurcate as it joins another black hole. We cannot break a black hole. But a black hole can break a black hole. The other answer is out of black hole cannot break another black hole. They just stick together like huge magnets, and it may take x number of Sagittarius A type bodies piled together before The integrity of any supermassive black hole breaks down. To the observer, it's just a huge black hole, but in reality, it's more of a nucleus or two neodymium magnets stuck together, perhaps crushed together, but still not one. I'm happy to say that I don't know.

Author: @lightningx10
Content:
This video is far too oversimplified and from what I can tell uses really weird terminology/notation. Quantim objects are NOT WAVES OR PARTICLES, to refer to a "liquid vacuum" and "nothing" as a physical thing is stupid, what you are referring to are quantum fields no?

As someone studying quantum physics, this video actively confused me just because of the incorrect naming and oversimplification. Not everything has a perfect analogy, and it's dishonest in my opinion to portray these "gravastars" in this way.

Another issue that you didn't even mention is that these gravastars do have a singularity. By having zero temperature on their shell, the shell's momentum would have no uncertainty and would be fixed at zero in some frames of reference. The uncertainty principle shows us that this is literally impossible, as the uncertainty in position would then be infinite, and you could never know precisely where a gravastar even is.

We can't begin to understand black holes or "gravastars" until we get some model of quantum gravity. Until then, this is completely meaningless conjecture and actively misleading to the general public.

A concrete example of the results of oversimplification can be found in other's comments about "the aether being back", or "pilot wave theory" making sense. These things are not coming back and that obviously can't be what you meant, but your oversimplified description lead people to misunderstand.

Very disappointed.
